title:
Rabbi Moses Sofer: Shaping the Character of Orthodox Judaism in Modernity

Rabbi Moses Sofer (known by the acronym Hatam Sofer, 1762–1839) was among the most prominent halakhic authorities and spiritual leaders of Central European Jewry in the early nineteenth century. He served as rabbi and rosh yeshiva in Pressburg (Bratislava) and wielded decisive influence on the formation of Orthodox Judaism as a distinct movement that arose in response to the challenges of modernity and the Haskalah.

Born in Frankfurt am Main, Sofer studied under Rabbi Nathan Adler and Rabbi Pinchas Horowitz. In 1806 he was appointed rabbi of Pressburg, where he established a yeshiva that became one of the most important centers of Torah study in Central Europe. Hundreds of students studied at the yeshiva, many of whom became leading rabbis and halakhic authorities in Jewish communities throughout the region.

Sofer's halakhic approach was characterized by extreme stringency and uncompromising opposition to any innovation in religious practice. His famous dictum "hadash asur min ha-Torah" (novelty is forbidden by the Torah) became a foundational principle of Orthodox Judaism. He vigorously opposed the Reform movement and any attempt to modify the traditional Jewish way of life, including changes in synagogue liturgy, the introduction of sermons in the vernacular, and reforms in Jewish education.

Sofer's halakhic writings are collected in his responsa work Sheʾelot u-Teshuvot Hatam Sofer (Responsa of Hatam Sofer), which encompasses thousands of responsa on all areas of halakha. He also authored Torat Mosheh (The Teaching of Moses), a commentary on the Torah, and Derashot Hatam Sofer (Sermons of Hatam Sofer), a collection of homiletical discourses. His writings reflect profound Talmudic erudition combined with sensitivity to the social and spiritual challenges facing the Jewish community in his time.

Sofer's influence extended far beyond the boundaries of his city and generation. His students disseminated his approach throughout Jewish communities in Hungary, Moravia, and Galicia, and his rulings were accepted as authoritative in Orthodox circles. He is considered one of the architects of ultra-Orthodox (Haredi) Judaism and his legacy continues to shape the worldview and halakhic practice of Orthodox communities to this day.

Rabbi Moses Sofer: Shaping the Character of Orthodox Judaism in the Modern Era

The text surveys the revolutionary teaching of Rabbi Moses Sofer, the "Hatam Sofer," who shaped the face of Orthodox Judaism as an active and militant response to the challenges of modernity and Reform in the nineteenth century. The article describes his life story from Germany to the establishment of the Torah center in Pressburg, while emphasizing his central ideology, "ḥadash asur min ha-Torah" (innovation is forbidden by the Torah), which sanctifies traditional custom as a spiritual defensive wall. Alongside extreme conservatism, the source reveals a complex leadership figure who combined phenomenal halakhic erudition with a positive attitude toward sciences serving the sacred and a deep connection to the settlement of Eretz Yisrael. In conclusion, the work traces the long-term legacy of the architect of Jewish conservatism, who established generations of students and descendants who continue his institutional and intellectual path to this day.

The Teaching, Activity, and Thought of Rabbi Moses Sofer: Shaping the Character of Orthodox Judaism in the Modern Era

The Historical and Cultural Background to the Rise of the Hatam Sofer

The second half of the eighteenth century and the first half of the nineteenth century constituted one of the most turbulent and formative periods in the history of the Jewish people in Europe. This was a period of sharp transition from the Middle Ages to modernity, a time when the old communal structures began to crumble under the pressures of emancipation, the Haskalah movement, and the beginnings of religious Reform.[1, 2] Within this maelstrom stood Rabbi Moses Sofer, known by his epithet the "Hatam Sofer" after his monumental series of works, as a central figure who succeeded not only in preserving what existed but in reinventing Jewish conservatism as an active and militant force.[1, 3]

The Hatam Sofer operated at the meeting point between the old world, represented by the autonomous communities and unshaken tradition, and the new world promising equal rights in exchange for relinquishing a distinctive religious identity.[1, 2] During this period, called the era of "the first fruits of emancipation," the physical and spiritual walls that separated Jews from their gentile surroundings were broken.[1] The changes were not only political but also matters of consciousness; the Haskalah movement placed human reason at the center, thereby undermining the absolute authority of halakhah and tradition.[2] The Hatam Sofer identified the danger inherent in these processes not only on the practical plane of observing the commandments, but on the deeper plane of the national and religious identity of the Jewish people.[2]

Formative Years in Frankfurt and the Influence of His Teachers

Moses Sofer was born in the year 5523 (1762) in Frankfurt am Main, one of the most important and traditional communities in Germany.[1] His family maintained a tradition of scribes of sacred texts (sofrei stam), a profession that gave him his family name, although in vernacular languages he was recorded as "Schreiber."[1] His family lineage was impressive and included key figures in the history of Jewish literature, such as the author of the Yalqut Shimoni and Rashi, as well as Rabbi Samuel Shotten Katz, called the Maharshashakh.[1] This lineage granted him a foundation of inherited authority, but it was his personal genius that stood out already in his childhood. By age seven he was already considered one who innovates original Torah insights (ḥiddushim), a characteristic that accompanied him throughout his life as a decisor (posek) and preacher.[1]

The most decisive influence on the Hatam Sofer came from his teachers in Frankfurt, foremost among them Rabbi Nathan Adler. Rabbi Nathan was an exceptional figure who combined traditional Talmudic scholarship with deep engagement in Kabbalah and Hasidic-ascetic customs, something that aroused fierce opposition among the communal establishment in Frankfurt.[1] The connection between the Hatam Sofer and Rabbi Nathan Adler was so deep that when the rabbi was forced to leave his city due to communal persecution, his young student accompanied him in his wanderings.[1] This experience of devotion to the rabbi against an opposing establishment shaped in the Hatam Sofer the conception of the spiritual leader as one who stands firm against external pressures, and the importance of preserving distinctive customs even when they seem strange to the surroundings.[1, 2] Another rabbi who influenced him was Rabbi Pinchas Horowitz, author of the Hafla'ah, who was a model figure of classical Ashkenazic scholarship combined with the Mussar movement and early Hasidism.[1]

The Rabbinical Career and the Move to Pressburg

After years of study and wanderings, the Hatam Sofer began to serve in official rabbinical positions. He served as rabbi in Dresnitz and later in Mattersdorf, one of the "seven communities" (Siebengemeinden) in Burgenland.[4] During these periods his name began to precede him as a sharp decisor of stature, as well as a rosh yeshivah attracting many students.[1] In the year 1806 (5566) came the great turning point in his career with his election to the rabbinate of the city of Pressburg (Bratislava), a position he held for thirty-three years until his death in 1839.[1, 2, 5]

Pressburg was at that time a vibrant and important Jewish center in the Kingdom of Hungary, and it provided the Hatam Sofer with the appropriate platform for disseminating his teaching.[5] Under his leadership, the community experienced unprecedented spiritual flourishing. He was not only a halakhic authority but also a public leader who dealt with dramatic historical events, such as the siege of the city during the Napoleonic Wars.[1] In his work Sefer Zikaron (Book of Remembrance), he describes in detail the tribulations suffered by members of the community and his leadership intervention to save them, something that attests to his deep involvement in the daily lives of his flock.[1]

The Pressburg Yeshivah: The Pedagogical and Organizational Revolution

One of the most important enterprises of the Hatam Sofer was the establishment and consolidation of the Pressburg yeshivah as the leading Torah center in Europe.[5] The yeshivah, which initially numbered only dozens of students, grew rapidly under his leadership to approximately 250 students, and subsequently even more under the leadership of his descendants.[5] The importance of the Pressburg yeshivah lay not only in the number of students but in the educational and organizational method that the Hatam Sofer charted, which became a model for many yeshivot throughout Hungary and Slovakia.[5, 7]

The Method of Study: "Study on the Page" and "According to the Halakhah"

The Hatam Sofer categorically opposed the method of empty pilpul that was prevalent in some yeshivot, in which emphasis was placed on intellectual acuity without binding connection to the plain meaning (peshat) of the text.[1] In its place, he instituted a method of "study on the page" (limmud al daf), in which each tractate was studied from beginning to end with deep penetration to the root of the Talmudic problems through the words of the Rishonim.[5] The ultimate goal of study in the yeshivah was "le-asuqei shema'ata alibah de-hilkheta"—that is, to arrive at knowledge of the decided halakhah from understanding its sources in the Talmud and commentators.[7, 8]

The students in the yeshivah studied at a pace of approximately two folios of Gemara with commentators per week, with Wednesdays devoted to review and Thursdays to oral examinations before the rosh yeshivah.[9] In addition, there was faster study for broad knowledge (beqi'ut) that included Rashi and Tosafot, as well as study of the Shulḥan Arukh and Pentateuch with commentators in the evening hours.[9] On Fridays the Hatam Sofer would give a special lesson on the weekly Torah portion, in which he combined the plain meaning with theological and ideological ideas.[9]

The Yeshivah as an Autonomous and Generational-Shaping Institution

The Pressburg yeshivah operated as an autonomous institution, without interference from the local community, which enabled the Hatam Sofer to dictate high standards of admission and study.[5] The students who were accepted were generally eighteen to nineteen years old who had already studied in other yeshivot, thereby making the yeshivah an institution for advanced Torah education that established the next generation of leadership of European Jewry.[5, 9] The Hatam Sofer required his students appointed to rabbinical positions to establish a yeshivah in their new community, thus creating an extensive network of yeshivot in the "Pressburg method" that preserved Orthodox identity.[2, 7]

"Innovation Is Forbidden by the Torah": The Conservative Ideology

The principle most identified with the teaching of the Hatam Sofer is "ḥadash asur min ha-Torah" (innovation is forbidden by the Torah).[2, 10] This expression, whose halakhic origin is in the prohibition of eating new grain before the omer offering, was borrowed by the Hatam Sofer to express sweeping opposition to any change in religious customs and the tradition of Israel.[2, 5] This was not merely a decl
a specific halakhic question, but rather a complete worldview designed to protect Judaism against the processes of modernization and Reform.[2, 10]

The Struggle Against Reform and Changes in Prayer

The Hatam Sofer viewed even the slightest changes in the prayer liturgy or in synagogue customs as a dangerous breach that could lead to the collapse of the entire system.[2] He argued that the Reform movement did not seek merely religious corrections, but rather undermined the very existence of the people of Israel as a separate nation fulfilling God's commandments.[3, 11] Therefore, he adopted an uncompromising stance against any "correction" in religion, even if it had no direct halakhic prohibition in the Shulhan Arukh.[2, 12] A prominent example of this was his opposition to moving the bimah from its place in the center of the synagogue or to using foreign languages in prayer.[2]

The Sanctity of Custom and Its Status

A central innovation in the Hatam Sofer's teaching was the elevation of custom to the highest status, sometimes even above written halakhah.[13] He believed that the custom accepted among the people of Israel for generations upon generations was the living expression of Torah, and that the validity of halakhah itself derives from the power of living tradition.[13] According to his approach, custom is the "ultimate weapon" against modernity, because it anchors Judaism in a historical continuity that cannot be challenged by transient rationalism.[13] Meticulous preservation of customs, including those that seemingly lack deep foundations, became a hallmark of the Hungarian Orthodoxy that he shaped.[12, 13]

His Halakhic Teaching and Literary Works

The Hatam Sofer is considered one of the greatest poskim of all time, and his reputation spread throughout all Jewish communities.[1] His rulings were accepted without challenge, and even non-Jewish judges turned to him with questions concerning Jewish law.[1] His halakhic work is characterized by a combination of phenomenal erudition in all parts of Torah together with a realistic approach connected to lived reality.[1, 7]

She'elot u-Teshuvot Hatam Sofer

His main work in the field of halakhah is "She'elot u-Teshuvot Hatam Sofer" (Responsa of the Hatam Sofer), comprising seven volumes containing 1,225 responsa.[1] The responsa deal with all areas of life—from monetary and personal status law to questions arising from the technology and science of his time.[1] The Hatam Sofer used experiments and scientific investigations to clarify halakhic matters; for example, he studied the anatomy of animals to determine their kashrut and examined the measurements appearing in halakhah.[1]

His Principal Works

Hiddushei Hatam Sofer: theoretical novellae on the Talmud, which constitute the foundation for study in many yeshivot to this day.[1]

Torat Moshe: an extensive commentary on the Torah and the Five Megillot, in which he combines derash, aggadah, and ideological concepts.[1]

Derashot Hatam Sofer: a collection of sermons he delivered in Pressburg, containing the principles of his teaching on matters of faith, ethics, and public leadership.[1]

Tzava'at Moshe: a short but powerful ideological document in which he commands his sons and descendants to continue on the path of extreme conservatism and to distance themselves from any influence of the Reform movement.[1, 13]

Shirat Moshe: poems and piyyutim written according to kabbalistic secrets.[1]

Attitude Toward the Sciences, External Wisdom, and Work

Despite his image as an extreme conservative, the Hatam Sofer's attitude toward external wisdom and the practical world was complex and in part surprising.[1, 11] He did not reject science per se, but rather its use as a tool for undermining religion.[11]

Science in the Service of Halakhah: The Hatam Sofer viewed science as a vital auxiliary tool for understanding Torah. He encouraged the study of anatomy, mathematics, and astronomy to the extent that they were necessary for understanding complex halakhic matters.[1] According to his approach, the "sciences" are "apothecaries and cooks" for Torah.[11]

Attitude Toward Work and Livelihood: He expressed a positive attitude toward work and learning professions, especially in the Land of Israel, where he saw this as part of the commandment of settling the Land.[11] He opposed new initiatives only when they came from reformist tendencies of assimilation, but did not reject involvement in economic life per se.[11]

Opposition to Secular Studies in Schools: His struggle against secular studies in educational institutions stemmed from the concern that this integration would lead to diminishing the importance of Torah study and to the penetration of foreign modern values into the hearts of students.[2, 11]

Love of the Land of Israel and Redemption

The Hatam Sofer is considered one of the greatest "lovers of the Land" of his period, and his conception regarding the Land of Israel was revolutionary and innovative.[2, 11] He believed that the primary fulfillment of Torah and commandments is in the Land of Israel, and compared life outside the Land to existence within a "grave."[11]

According to his teaching, work in the Land of Israel, and especially agricultural labor, is a supreme religious commandment.[11] He argued that the Shekhinah dwells in the Land through concrete action of building, and not only through theoretical Torah study.[11] This influence was evident among his disciples, some of whom immigrated to the Land of Israel and established the Old Yishuv in Jerusalem based on these principles.[2] He viewed emancipation in Europe as a worrying sign that the Jews might forget the hopes for national redemption in Zion and settle in exile, and therefore related to it with ambivalence.[2] His famous parable about the "king's son" who weeps when his father builds him a palace in exile illustrates the concern that material improvements in foreign lands would distance the nation from the vision of return to the Land.[2]

The Legacy and the Sofer-Schreiber Dynasty

The Hatam Sofer's death in 1839 did not mark the end of his influence, but rather the beginning of a rabbinic and spiritual dynasty that led Orthodoxy in Central Europe for more than a century.[6, 7] The communal and educational structure he established in Pressburg survived and expanded, as his descendants and disciples carried the torch of his teaching.[5, 6]

Continuators of His Path in Leadership

Rabbi Avraham Shmuel Binyamin Sofer (the "Ketav Sofer"): The Hatam Sofer's eldest son, who filled his father's position in the rabbinate of Pressburg and as head of the yeshivah.[6] He succeeded in preserving the yeshivah's status as a world Torah center and even increased the number of its students to approximately 400.[5] Under his leadership, the yeshivah was recognized by the Austro-Hungarian authorities as an institution of higher learning for the rabbinate.[5]

Rabbi Shimon Sofer (the "Mikhtav Sofer"): His second son, who served as rabbi of Kraków and was a key figure in rabbinic leadership in Poland and Galicia, while integrating his father's teaching with the needs of the large communities in the East.[6]

Rabbi Akiva Sofer (the "Da'at Sofer"): The Hatam Sofer's great-grandson, who continued the dynasty in Pressburg until the outbreak of World War II, when he immigrated to the Land of Israel and reestablished the Pressburg Yeshivah in Jerusalem, thereby ensuring the continuity of the enterprise even after the destruction of European Jewry.[6]

Long-Term Influence: The Invention of Orthodoxy as a Movement

The Hatam Sofer did not merely preserve traditional Judaism; he reshaped it as "Orthodoxy"—a self-conscious movement standing in confrontation with modern alternatives.[2] During his period, the poles were created within Hungarian Jewry that marked the way for the rest of Europe: the Orthodox who are meticulous about custom on one hand, and the Neologists seeking reform on the other.[2] The process of separating the communities, which began through his inspiration, enabled halakhah-observant Judaism to survive as a cohesive group with independent institutions, something that was vital to its ability to withstand the currents of secularization.[2]

His teaching became the cornerstone of broad streams in today's Haredi world, which adopt his slogan "the new is forbidden by the Torah" as a guiding principle in all areas of life.[10] Nevertheless, analysis of his work teaches that alongside conservatism, the Hatam Sofer possessed a broad vision that also encompassed the revival of the nation in its land, the importance of knowledge and science for the needs of Torah, and the need for active and realistic public leadership.[1, 11] His figure remains to this day as a bridge between ancient Ashkenazic scholarship and the challenges of the modern world, and his legacy continues to resonate in study halls and in the spiritual leadership of the people of Israel.[1, 7]

Summary

Rabbi Moshe Sofer, the Hatam Sofer, was an exemplary figure who succeeded in combining uncompromising religious zealotry with broad historical and leadership vision.[7] He built a fortified wall around the world of Torah and custom,
Yet at the same time he prepared the ground for the continued existence of the people of Israel under the conditions of a new era.[1, 7] His work at the yeshiva of Pressburg, his halakhic rulings in his She'elot u-Teshuvot (responsa), and his spiritual testament, all constitute central pillars in the edifice of Orthodox Judaism.[1, 5, 13] The Hatam Sofer was not merely a posek of his generation, but an architect of generations, who shaped with his own hands the face of Judaism faithful to tradition in the face of the ravages of time.[1, 7]
